newsitem.title: MALI: Mali rail company plans new investment.
newsitem.headline: Mali rail company plans new investment.

text.p: Landlocked Mali's rail company, back in profit after a shakeup that touched the whole state sector, plans to invest in new track and to streamline handling of freight to and from the outside world.
The company, founded in 1960, also plans to launch a project in 1997 to end congestion at the capital Bamako's rail station.
The freight plan envisages setting up a new company with neighbour Senegal, which offers the most accessible seaport, and with private investors to manage international traffic.

"We have envisaged the creation of a subsidiary company for the management of international traffic within the framework of of the link between the Malian and the Senegalese lines," the state rail company's managing director Lassana Kone said.
The idea was to set up an autonomous body to speed up development of the link, particularly for freight, he told Reuters in an interview.

Under the plan, the two state rail companies will hold 20 percent each of the new company, private foreign investors about 33 percent, national investors 24 percent and staff of the two rail companies about four percent.
The project has not yet been opened to offers.
Kone said that there were no immediate plans to privatise the Malian National Rail Company (RCFM), which notched up profits in both 1994 and 1995.

It made a profit of 800 million CFA francs ($1.6 million) in 1995 on turnover of 11 billion CFA francs. In 1994 the profit was 600 million CFA on turnover of nine billion CFA. Before that it struggled to balance its finances and live without subsidies.
The company's 642-km (399-mile) line from Koulikoro via Bamako to the Senegalese border handles around one million tonnes a year or up to 40 percent of the country's total imports.
Under a restructuring plan, begun in 1992 as part of a shakeup of Mali's public sector, the national railway has cut its staff to 1,700 workers from 2,300. The target was 1,500.
"We had to work out our real needs, study the nature of each post with the target of 1,500 in view," Kone said.

At the same time, the company had to refocus its business, shedding certain activities. "In the catering sector, the buffets in stations and on trains were privatised along with those working in these sectors and we sub-contracted the work of the train inspectors plus security."
Drought-prone Mali, with a population of more than eight million, is one of the world's poorest nations. Cotton, cattle and gold are its main products.
It has been busily liberalising its economy in cooperation with the International Monetary Fund and the World Bank, which have given its reforms high marks.

Kone said that the company hoped to invest in new track over the next four to five years to increase the speed at which trains can travel. "We have an investment plan of almost 18 billion CFA francs, under which, if it comes to fruition, we will redo almost 500 km of track," he said.
"We have 37 kg rails and would like to (upgrade) to 46 kg, which will mean that the average speeds will be from 60 to 90 km an hour compared to 50 to 70 km an hour at present," he added.
The company has been talking to the World Bank, the Canadian and French government overseas development agencies and the Arab Development Fund.
He said that a plan to build a freight terminal at Korofina, an eastern district of Bamako, would begin in 1997.
($1 = 509 CFA francs)
